Theory: Matmul, dot product, vector/matrix norms, eigenvalues. Read 3Blue1Brown Essence of LA chapters 1-7 if rusty.
Code: Numpy: implement matmul from scratch (3 nested loops). Verify vs np.matmul on random 8×8.
Deliverable: Notes + matmul.py

Theory: Bayes theorem, Gaussian, MLE vs MAP. Why MLE = minimize neg log likelihood.
Math: Derive MLE for a Gaussian: estimate μ, σ² from n samples. Show MLE σ² is biased.
Deliverable: Paper derivation photographed

Theory: Partial derivatives, multivariate chain rule. Practice 3 deep chain-rule problems.
Math: Compute ∂L/∂W for L = ||Wx − y||² by chain rule.
Deliverable: 3 worked problems

Theory: What LR is. Sigmoid. Cross-entropy as MLE under Bernoulli. Why L2 helps. Platt scaling vs isotonic.
Math: Derive MLE → CE loss. Derive ∂CE/∂w. Show L2 regularization geometry.
Code: Numpy LR on a 2D dataset (no sklearn). Forward + backward + SGD.
Deliverable: Paper derivation + lr.py

Theory: Bias-variance tradeoff. Why L1 gives sparsity, L2 doesn't. Nested CV.
Math: Derive MSE = Bias² + Variance + Noise. Geometric argument for L1 vs L2.
Deliverable: Paper derivation

Theory: Forward pass = function composition. Backward pass = chain rule reversed.
Math: Write all gradients on paper for a 2-layer MLP with ReLU.
Code: Numpy only: forward + backward + SGD on XOR. Verify grads match torch.autograd.
Deliverable: backprop_numpy.py + XOR training curve

Theory: SVD: A=UΣVᵀ; singular values = √eigenvalues of AᵀA. Low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young). Why SVD underlies PCA, LSA, embeddings, and LoRA (ΔW is low-rank). PCA: directions of max variance = top eigenvectors of covariance. When PCA fails (nonlinear → t-SNE/UMAP). Truncated SVD for compression.
Math: Derive PCA: maximise wᵀΣw s.t. ‖w‖=1 → eigenvector of covariance (Lagrange multipliers). Show best rank-k approximation = top-k singular triplets (Eckart–Young). Relate SVD of X to eigendecomposition of XᵀX.
Code: Numpy: PCA from scratch (center → covariance → eigh → project to k dims) on a 3D→2D toy set. Verify variance-explained ratio. Compare to np.linalg.svd reconstruction error at rank k.
Deliverable: pca.py + Eckart–Young note

Theory: Why ReLU. What GELU approximates. SiLU = x·σ(x). Why dying ReLU happens.
Code: Implement ReLU, GELU, SiLU as Python functions. Compute on x=[-2,-1,0,1,2]. Plot.
Deliverable: activations.py + plot

Theory: Why softmax(x) needs max-subtraction. What overflow looks like.
Math: Derive ∂s_i/∂x_j = s_i(δ_ij − s_j). Verify Jacobian on 3-element example.
Code: Implement numerically stable softmax. Compare to naive on x=[1000,1001,1002]. Backward pass manually.
Deliverable: softmax.py + paper derivation

Theory: CE vs log-loss vs log-likelihood (same thing). Why CE is right for classification.
Math: Derive ∂CE/∂logits = softmax − one_hot. (The clean form.)
Code: Implement CE from scratch. Verify against F.cross_entropy. Implement gradient manually.
Deliverable: ce_loss.py + numerical test

Theory: SGD vs momentum vs RMSProp vs Adam vs AdamW. Why decoupled weight decay matters.
Math: Write Adam update rule. Show bias correction.
Code: Implement Adam in numpy. Train your XOR MLP with it. Compare to SGD.
Deliverable: adam.py + comparison plot

Theory: Why warmup. Why cosine decay.
Code: get_lr(step, max_lr, min_lr, warmup, total). Plot curve for warmup=100, total=1000.
Deliverable: lr_schedule.py + plot

Theory: Why deep nets without residuals fail to train. Highway intuition.
Math: Show dx_L/dx_l = 1 + (...). Trace gradient for 4-layer residual net on paper.
Deliverable: Paper derivation

Theory: Entropy H(p)=-Σp·log p. Cross-entropy H(p,q). KL(p‖q)=H(p,q)−H(p) ≥ 0, asymmetric. Mutual information. Why CE is the LM loss. Perplexity PPL=exp(CE) = 'effective branching factor'. Bits-per-byte. Label smoothing = CE with soft targets.
Math: Show KL ≥ 0 (Gibbs/Jensen). Derive PPL=exp(CE); interpret PPL=10. Relate CE minimisation to MLE. Compute PPL for a toy 4-token distribution.
Code: Implement entropy, cross_entropy, kl_div, perplexity in numpy. Verify KL(p‖q) ≠ KL(q‖p). Compute PPL of a tiny LM's next-token distribution.
Deliverable: infotheory.py + PPL note

Theory: Walk through 3 merge steps on 'low lower newest widest'. Why 'lower' and 'low' separate. OOV handling. Vocab 32k vs 128k tradeoffs (memory, coverage, seq length).
Code: BPE tokenizer from scratch: count_pairs → find max → merge → repeat N. Encode greedy. Decode reverse. Verify round-trip on a paragraph.
Deliverable: bpe.py + round-trip test

Theory: WordPiece (likelihood) vs BPE (frequency). SentencePiece language-agnostic. Unigram pruning. Why BERT uses '##'.
Deliverable: Notes file

Theory: Embedding matrix shape for GPT-2. Why tie input emb with LM output head (param savings + better gradients). √d scaling.
Math: Show that weight tying halves embedding+head params for GPT-2 (vocab=50257, d=768).
Code: Implement Embedding module. Verify tied weights produce same forward as untied with copied weights.
Deliverable: embed.py + param count

Theory: Skip-gram vs CBOW. Negative sampling (why, vs full softmax; noise ∝ f^0.75). Hierarchical softmax. GloVe: factorise log co-occurrence matrix. Why static embeddings fail on polysemy → contextual (BERT). Analogy arithmetic (king−man+woman≈queen).
Math: Write skip-gram negative-sampling loss = −log σ(v_c·v_w) − Σ_neg log σ(−v_c·v_n). Show it is implicit PMI matrix factorisation (Levy & Goldberg).
Code: Numpy skip-gram with negative sampling on a toy corpus. Train, then check nearest neighbours by cosine similarity.
Deliverable: word2vec.py + neighbours demo

Theory: Attention(Q,K,V) formula. What Q, K, V represent. Causal mask = -inf before softmax. Softmax temperature.
Math: PROVE √d_k: with Q,K ~ N(0,1), Var(QKᵀ) = d_k → softmax saturates without scaling. Show what happens at d_k=64 without scaling.
Code: Implement attention with causal mask. Test with and without mask. Verify shapes [B,H,S,d]. Compare to F.scaled_dot_product_attention.
Deliverable: attention.py + paper proof

Theory: 4 weight matrices W_Q/W_K/W_V/W_O. Why multiple heads (different representation subspaces). Why not one head with d_model dims.
Math: Compute total MHA params for GPT-3 (d=12288, h=96 heads). Show 4·d² per layer.
Code: Implement complete MHA from scratch (no nn.MultiheadAttention). split_heads, attend per head, concat, project out. Verify param count.
Deliverable: mha.py + param count

Theory: Why attention has nice gradients. Where dropout typically goes (after softmax).
Math: Trace gradient through softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)·V step by step.
Deliverable: Paper trace

Theory: PE(pos,2i) formula. Why different frequencies per dim. Max seq length sinusoidal can extrapolate to.
Math: Show PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos). Compute PE for pos=0,1,2 at d=4.
Deliverable: Paper derivation + computed PE

Theory: q_m = q · e^(imΘ). Θ_j = base^(-2j/d). What rotate_half does. base 10000 → 500000 for LLaMA-3.
Math: Derive that q_m · k_n in the dot product depends only on (m−n), not m and n separately.
Code: Implement RoPE: precompute_freqs_cis + apply_rotary_emb. Verify q[m=5]·k[n=3] == q[m=8]·k[n=6] (same relative distance).
Deliverable: rope.py + relative position test

Theory: ALiBi bias formula. m_h slopes. Why ALiBi generalizes to longer sequences without training. LLaMA/Mistral/MPT/BLOOM PE choices.
Deliverable: Comparison table notes

Theory: How to extend pretrained context length. NTK formula. YaRN. Position interpolation.
Math: θ_new = θ_old · (L_test/L_train)^(d/(d-2)). Compute new base for LLaMA-2 (4096 → 32k).
Deliverable: Paper derivation + calc

Theory: What γ, β learn. Number of learnable params for d=4096. Why ε.
Math: Derive dL/dx = (γ/σ)·[dL/dy − mean(dL/dy) − x̂·mean(dL/dy·x̂)]. The tricky bit: μ and σ both depend on x.
Code: Implement LayerNorm from scratch (no F.layer_norm). Match torch to 1e-6.
Deliverable: layernorm.py + paper derivation

Theory: What term is dropped vs LN. Why faster. LLaMA/Mistral/Gemma all use it.
Math: Write the formula. Compare param count to LN.
Code: Implement RMSNorm. Match a reference within 1e-6.
Deliverable: rmsnorm.py

Theory: Draw both. Why Post-LN (original) unstable at init. Why Pre-LN trains. Which models use which.
Math: Trace gradient flow in Pre-LN vs Post-LN for a 32-layer model.
Deliverable: Notes + gradient trace

Theory: (xW₁ ⊙ SiLU(xW_gate))·W₂. Why 8/3·d_model hidden (not 4×). What gating does.
Math: Show 8/3 scaling preserves param count vs vanilla FFN with 4× hidden.
Code: Implement SwiGLU. Drop into your transformer block.
Deliverable: swiglu.py + param math

Theory: Pre-LN → MHA → residual → Pre-LN → SwiGLU → residual. Param count per block.
Math: Count params for d=4096, h=32, 8 KV heads.
Code: Implement full block. Verify gradients flow, no NaN after 10 steps. Output shape [B,S,D] preserved.
Deliverable: block.py + grad test

Theory: Embeddings + N blocks + RMSNorm + LM head (weight tied). Initialization scheme N(0, 0.02).
Math: Verify total params for GPT-2 small (12 layers, d=768, h=12, vocab=50257) ≈ 117M.
Code: Stack your block, add LM head with weight tying. Forward returns logits [B,S,vocab].
Deliverable: gpt.py + param count

Theory: What each does. Why nucleus sampling. Temperature effect.
Code: Implement top_k_sample, top_p_sample with temperature. Test temp=0.01 ≈ greedy, temp=2.0 chaotic. Build generate().
Deliverable: sampling.py + ablation

Theory: When beam > greedy. Why beam loses to nucleus in open-ended generation.
Code: beam_search(model, ids, width=5, max_len=50). Handle EOS. Verify beam=1 matches greedy.
Deliverable: beam_search.py + test

Theory: Why decoding without KV cache is O(n²) per step. Prefill vs decode distinction.
Math: Derive total decode compute with vs without cache.
Code: Modify your block to accept and return past_key_values. Pre-fill stores K,V; decode appends. Verify outputs identical with/without cache. Benchmark 10 steps, seq=100 → expect 10× speedup.
Deliverable: kv_cache.py + benchmark

topic: BERT vs GPT vs T5 + pretraining objectives
_source:
Theory: Encoder (BERT, bidirectional, MLM 15% + NSP) vs decoder (GPT, causal LM) vs enc-dec (T5/BART, span corruption / denoising). ELECTRA (replaced-token detection — more sample-efficient). Prefix-LM. When each wins (BERT: classification/retrieval; GPT: generation; T5: seq2seq). Why decoder-only + scale won.
Code: — (build comparison table + rehearse a 60s 'why decoder-only won' answer)
Deliverable: Comparison table + 60s answer

Theory: Why KV cache is the inference bottleneck. MQA shares one K,V across heads. GQA = G groups.
Math: Derive KV cache bytes = 2·L·S·G·d_h·dtype. Compute for LLaMA-2 70B (L=80, G=8, d_h=128, S=4096, batch=8, fp16). MQA reduction factor = H. GQA factor = H/G.
Code: Modify MHA to support num_kv_heads != num_heads. K,V output fewer heads, repeat_interleave to match Q. Verify shapes + memory saving.
Deliverable: gqa.py + memory calc

Theory: Standard attention IO = O(n²). FA IO = O(n²d/M), M = SRAM size. Why HBM is the bottleneck.
Math: Derive O(n²d/M). Explain online softmax: m=max(m₁,m₂), ℓ recurrence, O update. Compute speedup for A100 M=100KB, d=128, n=2048 (~26× fewer HBM accesses).
Deliverable: Paper derivation + speedup calc

Theory: Tiling strategy. Forward + backward recompute. FA-2 work partitioning. FA-3 async ops.
Deliverable: Notes + sketch

Theory: Why traditional KV cache wastes 60% memory. Block table maps (seq, logical_block) → physical_block. Memory util 95%+.
Math: Draw block table for 3 sequences (lengths 35, 20, 45, block_size=16).
Code: Simulate BlockAllocator in Python: allocate/free/copy_on_write. 5 sequences, lengths 10-100, block_size=16. Verify no two seqs share physical blocks except CoW.
Deliverable: block_allocator.py + diagram

Theory: Longformer sliding window + global → O(n). Performer FAVOR+ kernel. Linformer low-rank. When sparse over FA in 2025.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: GEMM (M×K)×(K×N) = 2MKN FLOPs. Forward + backward ≈ 6ND.
Math: Count FLOPs per op: QKV proj, scores QKᵀ, AV, FFN. Total L layers. Verify within 5% of 6ND for GPT-2 small.
Code: Build flop_counter(L, D, H, S, vocab) function. Test for LLaMA-7B at S=2048.
Deliverable: flop_counter.py + verification

Theory: weights=2P, grads=2P, AdamW=12P → 16P bytes (no activations). ZeRO-3 sharding.
Math: Compute training memory for 7B model. ZeRO-3 on 8 GPUs → 14GB/GPU.
Code: Build llm_memory(params_B, dtype, seq, layers, kv_heads, d_head, batch). Verify LLaMA-2 7B and 70B cases.
Deliverable: mem_calc.py + cases

Theory: bf16 vs fp16 (no scaler needed for bf16). When to clip. Gradient checkpointing tradeoff (≈1/√N memory).
Code: Full training loop: autocast bf16, GradScaler, grad clip, cosine LR, log loss/grad_norm/lr. Add torch.utils.checkpoint on transformer block. Verify peak memory drops.
Deliverable: train.py + ckpt benchmark

Theory: D_opt = 20·N. Why GPT-3 was undertrained. Implications for choosing model size vs data.
Math: Derive D_opt = 20·N. For compute budget 10²³ FLOPs, find optimal N, D. Was GPT-3 (175B, 300B tokens) over or undertrained?
Deliverable: Paper derivation + analysis

Theory: When LoRA vs full FT. Compute, generalization, multi-adapter serving, memory.
Deliverable: 60s framework answer

Theory: ΔW = BA. Init: A ~ N(0, σ²), B = 0. α/r scaling factor.
Math: Show BA = 0 at init. Show after 1 gradient step B becomes nonzero. Compute LoRA params = r·(d_in + d_out). For 7B all-linear at r=16, ≈ 0.6%.
Deliverable: Paper derivation + param math

Code: LoRALinear class: freeze base, add BA adapters with α/r. merge_weights() folds LoRA into base. Apply to your transformer (MHA + FFN). Only LoRA params in optimizer; <2% trainable.
Deliverable: lora.py + merge fn

Theory: Why user turns must have loss=-100. What happens if you don't mask.
Code: Implement chat-format tokenizer + loss mask. Verify only assistant tokens contribute to loss.
Deliverable: chat_mask.py + test

topic: QLoRA — NF4 + double quant + paged optim
_source:
Theory: Quantise the frozen base to 4-bit NF4 (information-theoretically optimal for ~N(0,1) weights); compute LoRA adapters in bf16. Double quantisation (quantise the quant constants). Paged optimisers (page 8-bit AdamW state to CPU on spikes). Why 4-bit base + bf16 adapters preserves quality. Owns your H100 27B memory story.
Math: Compute memory: 7B in NF4 ≈ 3.5GB base + LoRA r=16 + paged 8-bit AdamW, vs a full bf16 fine-tune (~112GB). Show adapter params < 0.5%.
Code: Extend your LoRALinear to wrap an NF4-simulated base (fake-quant to nearest NF4 level, dequant on forward). Verify forward ≈ bf16 within tolerance; only adapters in the optimizer.
Deliverable: qlora.py + memory table

Theory: Preference data format. Reward hacking with 3 examples. Inter-annotator agreement.
Math: Derive BT loss = -log σ(r(x,y_w) − r(x,y_l)). Show loss decreases as r_w − r_l grows.
Code: Implement rm_loss(r_chosen, r_rejected). Verify decreases on synthetic data.
Deliverable: rm_loss.py + writeup

Theory: Why KL to ref policy. β controls deviation. β → 0 vs β → ∞.
Math: Derive: max_π E[r(x,y)] − β·KL(π || π_ref). Show optimal π*(y|x) ∝ π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x,y)/β).
Deliverable: Paper derivation

Theory: Why DPO simplifies RLHF (no RL, no separate RM). When DPO underperforms PPO.
Math: STEP-BY-STEP: start from RLHF max → optimal π* → express r in terms of π*, π_ref → substitute into BT loss → arrive at DPO loss. Do this twice cold.
Deliverable: Full paper derivation

Theory: Typical β = 0.1-0.5. Implicit reward r = β·log(π_θ/π_ref).
Code: Implement dpo_loss(policy_chosen_logps, policy_rejected_logps, ref_chosen_logps, ref_rejected_logps, beta). Verify loss decreases as chosen > rejected gap grows.
Deliverable: dpo_loss.py + verify

topic: DPO vs PPO vs ORPO vs SimPO
_source:
Theory: Comparison table: needs_ref_model, data format, compute, key advantage. 60s answer per method.
Deliverable: Comparison table + rehearsed answer

Theory: Self-critique loop. AI feedback vs human. Where it differs from RLHF.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: Full RLHF loop: SFT → reward model → PPO. Actor (policy) + critic (value head) + frozen ref + RM. Clipped surrogate objective. GAE for advantages. Per-token KL penalty to ref (reward = RM score − β·KL). Why PPO is unstable/expensive → motivates DPO. Value-head initialisation.
Math: Write the clipped objective L=E[min(r_t·A_t, clip(r_t,1−ε,1+ε)·A_t)], r_t=π_θ/π_old. Write GAE: A_t=Σ(γλ)^l δ_{t+l}. Show clipping bounds the policy update.
Code: Implement ppo_clip_loss(logp_new, logp_old, advantages, eps) + a GAE function. Verify clipping activates when the ratio leaves [1−ε, 1+ε].
Deliverable: ppo.py + objective derivation

Theory: Per-tensor vs per-channel vs per-group. Outlier-aware (SmoothQuant). Where errors come from.
Math: scale = max(|x|)/127. Round-trip error ≈ scale/2. Compute error for N(0,1) input.
Code: Implement quantize_symmetric + dequantize. Per-channel version. Round-trip error < 1% on N(0,1). Benchmark on a LLaMA linear layer.
Deliverable: int8.py + error measure

Theory: GPTQ: optimal brain quant (Hessian-based). AWQ: activation-aware. Tradeoffs. When each.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: AI = FLOPs / bytes_accessed. A100 ridge = 156 FLOPs/byte. Prefill compute-bound, decode memory-bound.
Math: Derive prefill AI ≈ S/2. Derive decode AI ≈ 0.5. Find break-even batch size where decode becomes compute-bound on A100.
Deliverable: Paper derivation + plot

Theory: TTFT ≈ (12L·D²·S) / GPU_FLOPS. TPOT ≈ weights_bytes / GPU_BW. When latency budget is blown.
Math: Compute TTFT for 7B, S=512, A100 (312 TFLOPS, 50% MFU). Compute TPOT for 70B fp16 TP=4 on A100.
Code: Roofline analyzer + latency estimator. Match theoretical within 10%.
Deliverable: roofline.py + latency.py

Theory: Draft model + target. Accept/reject sampling. When the speedup pays off.
Math: Prove min(1, q(t)/p(t)) preserves target distribution. Speedup E[speedup] = (1-α^(k+1))/(1-α) / (1+k·c). Compute for α=0.8, k=4, c=0.1.
Code: Implement accept/reject sampling. Verify output distribution matches target (KL < 0.01 over 10k samples).
Deliverable: spec_dec.py + KL test

Theory: Iteration-level (continuous) batching vs static batching — why static wastes GPU on ragged lengths. Prefill vs decode; chunked prefill. Prefix caching. PagedAttention block manager (ties to your block_allocator). Scheduler: waiting/running/swapped queues, preemption via recompute vs swap. SGLang RadixAttention (prefix-tree KV sharing). Throughput vs latency tradeoff. Contrast TGI / TensorRT-LLM.
Math: Estimate throughput gain of continuous vs static batching for a batch with high length variance; show the GPU-utilisation improvement (idle-slot elimination).
Code: Simulate a continuous-batching scheduler in Python: a step loop that admits new requests each iteration, runs one decode step per active seq, evicts finished seqs, and respects a KV-block budget (reuse your BlockAllocator). Log batch occupancy over time.
Deliverable: cont_batch_sim.py + scheduler notes

Theory: Given model size, SLO, QPS → GPU count. Connects memory + AI + TPOT.
Code: capacity_planner(model_size, slo_ms, qps) → GPU count. Verify LLaMA-2 70B case.
Deliverable: capacity.py + cases

topic: PTQ vs QAT, FP8, KV-cache quant
_source:
Theory: PTQ (calibrate, no training) vs QAT (fake-quant in training with straight-through estimator). FP8 (E4M3 / E5M2) on Hopper — why the format matters. KV-cache quantisation (INT8/FP8 KV) for long context. When accuracy justifies QAT. Weight-only vs weight+activation.
Math: Straight-through-estimator gradient for fake-quant. Compare dynamic range vs precision of E4M3 vs E5M2 vs INT8.
Code: — (notes + a small STE fake-quant snippet)
Deliverable: Notes + STE snippet

Theory: RMSNorm + SwiGLU + RoPE + GQA. Per-version differences (context length, tokenizer, RoPE base, GQA ratio).
Code: Wire your block to match LLaMA-3 architecture exactly. Verify config matches HF llama-3-8b config.
Deliverable: Notes + config match

Theory: Top-k routing. Aux load-balance loss. Expert collapse problem.
Math: L_aux = α·n·Σ f_i·p_i. Prove L=0 iff uniform routing. Apply to Mixtral 8×7B compute math.
Code: Implement MoE layer with top-k routing + aux loss. Output shape correct; aux loss is scalar.
Deliverable: moe.py + aux derivation

Theory: Contrastive image-text training. Vision encoder + projection + LM. Training stages.
Math: InfoNCE / CLIP loss formula. Symmetric loss.
Code: Implement CLIP loss (InfoNCE). Symmetric, correct for batch of 4.
Deliverable: clip_loss.py + test

Theory: Selective state space. Why O(n) vs O(n²). When competitive with transformers.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: DP for batch, TP for big layers, PP for memory, SP for long context. When each.
Deliverable: Notes + decision tree

Theory: Optimizer/grad/param sharding stages. Memory savings per stage. Communication tradeoffs.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: Eff BW = α·(N-1)/N × link BW. Latency O(N) hops.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: TPU systolic array. JAX jit/vmap/pmap. XLA sharding (pjit, GSPMD).
Code: Minimal Flax GPT loop: model + optax + pjit train step + orbax checkpoint.
Deliverable: jax_gpt.py walkthrough

Theory: SM, warps (32 threads), memory hierarchy (registers → shared/SRAM → L2 → HBM). Occupancy, coalesced access, bank conflicts. Why FlashAttention tiles for SRAM. Triton programming model (blocks, program_id). TensorRT-LLM. Mainly for NVIDIA / Meta infra roles.
Code: Triton (or numpy pseudocode) fused softmax; explain the tile-size choice. Optional: tiled matmul sketch.
Deliverable: Notes + fused_softmax sketch

Theory: Bias reduction vs bagging. XGBoost split gain. Missing value handling. Why beats DL on tabular.
Math: Write gain formula.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: When AUC-ROC lies (imbalance) → PR-AUC. P/R, F1 vs Fβ. Log loss vs Brier. Micro vs macro.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: NDCG formula + why DCG alone fails. MAP, MRR. RMSE vs MAE robustness. Cohen's kappa.
Math: Derive NDCG.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: Target encoding leak + K-fold fix. Time-series vs random split. Cat: one-hot vs target vs embedding.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: CLT. Type I/II + power. Bonferroni vs BH. Bootstrap vs analytical CI. Bayesian vs frequentist.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: Sample size from MDE, α, β. SRM detection. Novelty effect. Peeking + mSPRT.
Math: Derive sample size formula n = (z_{α/2}+z_β)²·2σ²/Δ².
Deliverable: Notes + sample size calc

Theory: CUPED variance reduction. Marketplace interference. Triggered vs ITT. Guardrails vs north-star.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: ATE/ATT/CATE. IVs. Diff-in-diff. PSM caveats. Simpson's paradox example.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: User/item towers + dot product. In-batch negatives + logQ correction. Normalize embeddings. ANN serving.
Math: Derive BPR loss.
Deliverable: Notes + arch diagram

Theory: ScaNN anisotropic quant. HNSW graph + search. IVF + residual PQ. Recall/latency/memory at 1B vectors.
Deliverable: Comparison table

Theory: Wide (memorization) + Deep (generalization). DLRM: sparse emb + dense + interaction. Crosses explicit vs learned.
Deliverable: Notes + DLRM diagram

Theory: BPR loss. In-batch vs uniform vs mixed negatives. Hard negative mining. Popularity bias correction.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: ε-greedy vs UCB vs Thompson. Contextual bandits (LinUCB). Off-policy eval (IPS, doubly robust).
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: Offline (NDCG, Recall@K) vs online (CTR, dwell, retention) divergence. Popularity bias. Delayed feedback. Cold start.
Deliverable: Notes

Theory: Max-margin classifier. Hard vs soft margin (C). Hinge loss. Kernel trick (RBF, polynomial) — implicit feature map. Support vectors. Dual formulation intuition. When SVM vs logistic regression vs trees.
Math: Write primal (½‖w‖² + C·Σξ) and hinge loss. Show margin = 2/‖w‖. State the kernelised decision function.
Code: — (notes; optional sklearn SVM on toy 2D + plot decision boundary)
Deliverable: Notes + margin derivation

Theory: k-means (Lloyd's, k-means++, elbow/silhouette), GMM + EM, DBSCAN/HDBSCAN (density-based, no k, handles noise). PCA vs t-SNE vs UMAP (when each; t-SNE not for absolute distances). Anomaly detection: isolation forest, LOF, autoencoder reconstruction error. Ties to your Photos face-clustering design.
Math: Write the k-means objective (within-cluster SSE) and show Lloyd's monotonic decrease. GMM E-step / M-step at a high level.
Code: Numpy k-means (k-means++ init) on toy blobs; plot clusters + centroids; report inertia.

topic: What is LLM inference? Prefill vs decode
_source:
Theory: Autoregressive generation = one forward pass per token. Two phases: PREFILL (process the whole prompt in parallel, builds the KV cache, produces the 1st token) and DECODE (generate tokens one at a time, each attending to the cache). Why they have totally different performance characteristics. Where the time goes for short vs long prompts.
Math: For prompt length P and G generated tokens, show prefill does ~P tokens of compute once; decode does G sequential steps. Total forward passes = 1 (prefill) + G-1 (decode).
Code: — (draw the prefill→decode timeline and annotate what fills the KV cache at each step)
Deliverable: Prefill/decode timeline diagram

topic: Latency & throughput metrics (TTFT, TPOT, throughput, goodput)
_source:
Theory: TTFT (time-to-first-token) = prefill latency, user-perceived responsiveness. TPOT / ITL (inter-token latency) = per-token decode latency, streaming smoothness. E2E latency = TTFT + (G-1)·TPOT. Throughput = tokens/sec across all requests. Goodput = throughput that meets SLO. Why optimizing throughput can hurt TTFT (batching tradeoff).
Math: Write E2E = TTFT + (N_out-1)·TPOT. For TTFT SLO 500ms, TPOT SLO 50ms, 200 output tokens → E2E budget ≈ 10.5s. Show how batch size trades TTFT vs throughput.
Code: Implement a latency calculator: given TTFT, TPOT, output length → E2E; and given per-request latencies + SLOs → goodput fraction.
Deliverable: latency_metrics.py

topic: The central dichotomy: compute-bound vs memory-bound
_source:
Theory: The single most important idea in inference. Prefill = compute-bound (lots of matmul, high arithmetic intensity). Decode with batch=1 = memory-bandwidth-bound (you stream all weights from HBM to generate ONE token → GPU compute sits idle). This is why decode throughput scales with batching and with quantization, not with more FLOPs.
Math: Arithmetic intensity AI = FLOPs / bytes_accessed. Show decode batch=1 AI ≈ 0.5 (way below the ridge) → memory-bound. Show prefill AI ≈ S/2 → compute-bound above some S.
Code: — (write the 2-sentence explanation you'd give an interviewer for 'why is LLM decoding slow?')
Deliverable: 60s 'why decode is slow' answer

topic: GPU anatomy: SMs, tensor cores, warps
_source:
Theory: Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) = the parallel compute units. Warps = 32 threads executing in lockstep (SIMT). Tensor cores = matmul accelerators (the FLOPS that matter for LLMs). CUDA cores vs tensor cores. Occupancy = active warps / max. Why LLM inference is dominated by GEMMs on tensor cores.
Code: — (label a GPU block diagram: SM → warps → tensor/CUDA cores)
Deliverable: GPU anatomy notes

topic: Memory hierarchy & bandwidth (registers → SRAM → L2 → HBM)
_source:
Theory: Registers (fastest, tiny) → shared memory/SRAM (~KB-MB, per-SM, ~fast) → L2 (MB) → HBM (GB, the big one, the bottleneck). Bandwidth numbers: A100 HBM ≈ 2 TB/s, H100 ≈ 3.35 TB/s; SRAM is ~10-20× faster than HBM. Why FlashAttention exists: keep the n×n scores in SRAM, never write them to HBM.
Math: Compute how long it takes to read 14 GB of fp16 weights from A100 HBM: 14GB / 2TB/s = 7 ms. That is the floor on decode TPOT for a 7B model at batch=1.
Code: — (memory-hierarchy table with capacity + bandwidth per level)
Deliverable: Memory hierarchy table

Theory: Roofline: performance is min(peak_FLOPS, AI × peak_bandwidth). The 'ridge point' = peak_FLOPS / peak_BW separates memory-bound (left) from compute-bound (right). A100 ridge ≈ 312 TFLOPS / 2 TB/s = 156 FLOPs/byte. Anything with AI below 156 is memory-bound on A100. This one plot explains all inference optimization.
Math: Compute ridge point for A100 (156) and H100 (~1000 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s ≈ 300 FLOPs/byte). Plot where prefill and decode land on the roofline.
Code: Build a roofline_analyzer(flops, bytes, peak_flops, peak_bw) → bound type + achievable FLOPS. Verify it flags decode as memory-bound.
Deliverable: roofline.py + plot

Theory: MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) = achieved FLOPs / peak FLOPs — the right metric for compute-bound prefill/training. MBU (Model Bandwidth Utilization) = achieved BW / peak BW — the right metric for memory-bound decode. Why reporting MFU for decode is misleading. Typical real MFU 30-50%, MBU 60-80%.
Math: Given tokens/sec and model size, back out MBU = (params·bytes·tokens_per_sec)/peak_BW. Compute MBU for 7B fp16 at 140 tok/s on A100.
Code: — (add MFU/MBU output to your roofline tool)
Deliverable: MFU/MBU notes

Theory: Bytes per param and dynamic range/precision tradeoffs. FP16 (5-exp) vs BF16 (8-exp, no loss scaling) vs FP8 E4M3/E5M2 (Hopper) vs INT8/INT4 (integer, needs scale). Why weights in low precision cut both memory AND bandwidth → directly speeds up memory-bound decode. Accuracy cliffs.
Math: Tabulate bytes/param and represent-able range for each format. Show a 70B model: fp16=140GB, int8=70GB, int4=35GB → which fit on 1×/2×/8× 80GB GPUs.
Code: — (precision comparison table)
Deliverable: Precision table

topic: FLOP counting for a forward pass
_source:
Theory: A (M×K)·(K×N) GEMM = 2·M·K·N FLOPs. Forward pass ≈ 2·N·D FLOPs per token (N=params, D=tokens). Per-layer breakdown: QKV proj, attention scores, AV, output proj, FFN (dominant). Backward ≈ 2× forward, so training ≈ 6ND; inference forward-only ≈ 2ND.
Math: Count FLOPs per op for one transformer layer (d_model, n_heads, seq S). Sum over L layers. Verify total ≈ 2·N per token within 5% for GPT-2 small.
Code: flop_counter(L,D,H,S,vocab) for the forward pass; test on LLaMA-7B at S=2048.
Deliverable: flop_counter.py

Theory: Prefill is compute-bound: process all S prompt tokens in parallel. TTFT ≈ prefill_FLOPs / (peak_FLOPS · MFU). Scales ~linearly with prompt length (quadratically for the attention term at long context). Batching prompts increases throughput but each TTFT grows.
Math: TTFT ≈ (2·N·S)/(FLOPS·MFU). Compute TTFT for 7B, S=512, A100 (312 TFLOPS, 50% MFU) ≈ 12·L·D²·S/FLOPS. Show the long-context S² attention term overtaking.
Code: Add ttft_estimate() to your latency tool; compare to a measured vLLM prefill within 20%.
Deliverable: ttft.py + validation

Theory: Decode at batch=1 is bandwidth-bound: TPOT ≈ weights_bytes / (peak_BW · MBU). Independent of prompt length (KV read is small vs weights) until context is huge. Increasing batch amortizes the weight read across many sequences → higher throughput, same-ish TPOT until compute-bound.
Math: TPOT ≈ model_bytes / GPU_BW. 7B fp16 on A100 = 14GB/2TB/s = 7ms/tok. 70B fp16 TP=4 on A100 = (140/4)GB / 2TB/s ≈ 17.5ms/tok. Find the batch size where decode turns compute-bound.
Code: tpot_estimate(model_bytes, bw, batch); verify the 7B and 70B cases.
Deliverable: tpot.py

topic: Inference memory footprint: weights + KV + activations
_source:
Theory: Inference memory = weights (2P fp16) + KV cache (grows with batch × seq) + activations (small, transient) + framework overhead. Unlike training (16P for optimizer states), inference weights are just 2P. At scale the KV cache, not the weights, is what caps concurrency.
Math: Total = 2P + KV(batch,seq) + overhead. For 7B fp16: 14GB weights; at batch=32, seq=2048 KV can be another ~8-16GB. Compute max concurrent sequences on an 80GB GPU.
Code: llm_infer_memory(params_B, dtype, batch, seq, layers, kv_heads, d_head) → GB breakdown.
Deliverable: infer_mem.py + cases

topic: KV cache mechanics — why it exists
_source:
Theory: Without a cache, every decode step recomputes K,V for all previous tokens → O(n²) per step, O(n³) total. The KV cache stores past K,V so each new token only computes its own Q and attends to cached K,V → O(n) per step. This is THE core inference optimization and the source of the memory pressure everything else fights.
Math: Derive total decode compute with vs without the cache. Show cache turns per-step cost from O(n·d) recompute to O(d) new + O(n·d) attend.
Code: Add past_key_values to your GPT block: prefill stores K,V; decode appends. Verify outputs identical with/without cache; benchmark ~10× speedup over 10 steps.
Deliverable: kv_cache.py + benchmark

Theory: The number every inference interview wants. KV bytes = 2 · L · S · n_kv_heads · d_head · dtype_bytes · batch. (2 = K and V.) Grows linearly with batch AND sequence length — this is why long context and high concurrency are expensive, and why GQA + quantization target it.
Math: KV bytes = 2·L·S·G·d_h·dtype·B. Compute for LLaMA-2 70B (L=80, G=8, d_h=128, S=4096, fp16, B=8) ≈ 2·80·4096·8·128·2·8 ≈ 84 GB — larger than the 70B weights at that batch!
Code: kv_cache_bytes(L,S,kv_heads,d_head,dtype,batch); verify the 70B case.
Deliverable: kv_calc.py

topic: MQA & GQA — shrinking the KV cache
_source:
Theory: Multi-Query Attention: all query heads share ONE K,V head → KV cache shrinks by factor H. Grouped-Query Attention: G groups → shrink by H/G, a quality/memory compromise (LLaMA-2/3 use GQA). This directly raises max batch size and context length. Why quality holds up.
Math: KV reduction factor MQA = H; GQA = H/G. LLaMA-2 70B: 64 Q heads, 8 KV heads → 8× smaller KV cache vs full MHA.
Code: Modify MHA so num_kv_heads ≠ num_heads; repeat_interleave K,V to match Q. Verify shapes + the memory saving.
Deliverable: gqa.py + memory calc

Theory: Store the cache in INT8/FP8 instead of fp16 → 2× more context/batch for a small accuracy hit. Per-channel/per-token scales. Asymmetric for the outlier-heavy K. When it's worth it (long context, high concurrency). Tradeoffs vs GQA (they compose).
Math: Show KV quant halves KV bytes; recompute max concurrency for the 70B case with INT8 KV.
Code: Quantize the cache to INT8 in your decode path (fake-quant); measure accuracy delta on a short generation.
Deliverable: kv_quant.py

Theory: Traditional KV cache pre-allocates max_seq per request → ~60-80% wasted memory from internal + external fragmentation. PagedAttention (vLLM) stores KV in fixed-size blocks (e.g. 16 tokens) mapped by a block table (virtual→physical, like OS paging). Waste ≤ block_size-1 tokens → 95%+ utilization. Copy-on-write enables prompt/beam sharing.
Math: Draw a block table for 3 sequences (lengths 35, 20, 45; block=16). Show waste = block_size-1 per seq. Compute utilization gain vs pre-allocation.
Code: Simulate a BlockAllocator: allocate/free/copy_on_write for 5 sequences (len 10-100, block=16). Verify no two seqs share a physical block except under CoW.
Deliverable: block_allocator.py + diagram

Theory: Standard attention materializes the n×n scores in HBM → O(n²) memory traffic, the real bottleneck (not FLOPs). FlashAttention tiles Q,K,V into SRAM and computes softmax incrementally (online softmax) so it never writes the n×n matrix → O(n²d/M) HBM accesses (M=SRAM size). ~26× fewer HBM reads at n=2048, d=128, M=100KB.
Math: Derive IO = O(n²d/M). Write the online-softmax recurrence: m=max(m₁,m₂), ℓ=e^(m₁-m)ℓ₁+e^(m₂-m)ℓ₂, rescale O. Compute the HBM-access speedup for A100.
Code: — (paper derivation + speedup calc; optional numpy online-softmax that matches full softmax)
Deliverable: FA derivation + speedup

Theory: v1: tiling + recomputation in backward (trade compute for memory). v2: better work partitioning across warps, fewer non-matmul ops, ~2× faster. v3: Hopper async (TMA, warp-specialization, FP8). Why FA made long context practical. Backward pass recomputes the forward stats instead of storing them.
Code: — (one-paragraph 'what each FA version improved' + backward-recompute sketch)
Deliverable: FA versions notes

Theory: Long prompts make prefill a latency spike that blocks decode requests (head-of-line blocking). Chunked prefill splits a long prompt into chunks and interleaves them with ongoing decode steps in the same batch → smoother TPOT, better GPU utilization, tunable TTFT/throughput. Default in modern vLLM.
Math: Show how a 4096-token prefill split into 512-token chunks lets decode requests progress between chunks; estimate the TPOT jitter reduction.
Code: — (scheduling diagram: monolithic vs chunked prefill interleaved with decode)
Deliverable: Chunked-prefill diagram

topic: Static vs dynamic vs continuous (iteration-level) batching
_source:
Theory: Static batching: wait to fill a batch, all finish together → padding + head-of-line waste. Dynamic batching: pad to the longest in a time window. Continuous (iteration-level) batching (Orca/vLLM): the scheduler re-forms the batch EVERY decode step — finished sequences leave, new ones join immediately. Huge throughput win on ragged workloads.
Math: Estimate GPU-utilization gain of continuous vs static batching for a batch with high length variance (idle-slot elimination). Show why static wastes on the longest sequence.
Code: Simulate a continuous-batching loop: admit new requests each iteration, run 1 decode step per active seq, evict finished, respect a KV-block budget. Log batch occupancy over time.
Deliverable: cont_batch_sim.py

topic: Scheduler internals: queues, preemption, swap vs recompute
_source:
Theory: vLLM-style scheduler: waiting / running / swapped queues. When KV memory is full it PREEMPTS lower-priority sequences — either swap their KV to CPU (copy back later) or recompute (drop KV, redo prefill on resume). FCFS vs priority. Admission control to protect SLOs. Starvation avoidance.
Math: Compare swap (extra PCIe bandwidth, keep KV) vs recompute (extra FLOPs, free KV) cost; give the rule of thumb for when each wins.
Code: Extend your scheduler sim with a KV budget that triggers preemption; implement both swap and recompute strategies and compare.
Deliverable: scheduler_sim.py

Theory: Reuse the KV of a shared prompt prefix (system prompt, few-shot examples, chat history) across requests instead of recomputing prefill → big TTFT + throughput win for repeated prefixes. SGLang's RadixAttention stores KV in a radix tree keyed by token prefix; LRU eviction. Automatic in vLLM's prefix caching.
Math: For a 2000-token system prompt shared by 1000 requests, compute prefill FLOPs saved by caching the prefix once.
Code: Implement a radix/trie prefix cache: insert token sequences, match longest cached prefix, LRU-evict. Verify a repeated prefix hits the cache.
Deliverable: prefix_cache.py

Theory: Prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) contend for the same GPU and interfere. Disaggregation (Splitwise, DistServe) runs prefill on one pool of GPUs and decode on another, transferring the KV cache between them → each pool tuned for its regime, better goodput. The cost: KV transfer bandwidth.
Math: Sketch the KV-transfer cost between prefill and decode nodes; show when disaggregation beats co-location (high prefill/decode interference).
Code: — (architecture diagram: disaggregated prefill and decode pools + KV transfer)
Deliverable: Disagg diagram

Theory: Raw throughput is the wrong target — GOODPUT (requests served within SLO) is what matters. SLO-aware schedulers prioritize to maximize goodput: cap batch size to protect TTFT, reserve capacity for decode, admission-control under overload. TTFT vs TPOT vs throughput is a 3-way tradeoff you tune per product.
Math: Given per-request TTFT/TPOT and SLO thresholds, compute goodput; show how raising batch size increases throughput but drops goodput once TTFT SLO breaks.
Code: Add goodput measurement to your sim; sweep batch size and plot throughput vs goodput.
Deliverable: goodput.py + curve

Theory: Map fp values to int8 with a scale (and zero-point if asymmetric). Granularity: per-tensor (1 scale, coarse) → per-channel (1 per output) → per-group (1 per G weights, best accuracy). Outliers wreck per-tensor → per-channel/group or outlier handling. Weight-only cuts memory+BW (helps decode); activation quant also cuts compute.
Math: scale = max(|x|)/127; round-trip error ≈ scale/2. Compute error for N(0,1) input; show per-channel beats per-tensor.
Code: quantize_symmetric + dequantize, per-tensor and per-channel. Round-trip error < 1% on N(0,1); benchmark on a LLaMA linear layer.
Deliverable: int8.py + error measure

Theory: GPTQ: layer-wise, Hessian-based (Optimal Brain Quant) weight rounding → strong 4-bit weight-only. AWQ: activation-aware — protect the ~1% salient weight channels (scale by activation magnitude) → fast, accurate 4-bit. SmoothQuant: migrate activation outliers into weights so W8A8 works. When to use each.
Code: — (comparison table: method, W/A bits, calibration cost, accuracy, when to use)
Deliverable: GPTQ/AWQ/SmoothQuant table

topic: FP8, KV-cache quant, PTQ vs QAT
_source:
Theory: FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) on Hopper: near-fp16 quality at 2× throughput/memory. KV-cache quant for long context. Weight-only (decode BW) vs weight+activation (also prefill compute). PTQ (calibrate only) vs QAT (fake-quant in training with straight-through estimator) — QAT when PTQ accuracy is unacceptable.
Math: Straight-through-estimator gradient for fake-quant. Compare dynamic range vs precision of E4M3, E5M2, INT8.
Code: — (STE fake-quant snippet + notes)
Deliverable: PTQ/QAT/FP8 notes

topic: Sampling recap: greedy / top-k / top-p / temperature
_source:
Theory: How each shapes the output distribution and why it matters for latency (they're cheap, but repetition penalties and large vocabs add up). Temperature scaling, nucleus (top-p) sampling, top-k, min-p. Determinism (temp→0 ≈ greedy). Batched sampling on GPU.
Code: top_k_sample, top_p_sample with temperature; verify temp=0.01 ≈ greedy, temp=2.0 chaotic. Build generate().
Deliverable: sampling.py

Theory: A small fast DRAFT model proposes k tokens; the big TARGET verifies them in ONE forward pass; a rejection-sampling rule accepts a prefix that provably preserves the target distribution. Turns memory-bound decode into fewer, denser target passes → 2-3× speedup with no quality loss. Speedup depends on acceptance rate α and draft cost.
Math: Prove min(1, q(t)/p(t)) acceptance keeps the target distribution. E[speedup] = ((1-α^(k+1))/(1-α)) / (1+k·c). Compute for α=0.8, k=4, c=0.1 → ~3×.
Code: Implement accept/reject speculative sampling; verify output distribution matches the target (KL < 0.01 over 10k samples).
Deliverable: spec_decode.py + KL test

topic: Advanced speculation: Medusa, EAGLE, lookahead, n-gram
_source:
Theory: Self-speculation without a separate draft model. Medusa: extra decoding heads predict multiple future tokens + tree attention verifies. EAGLE: predict at the feature level (more accurate drafts). Lookahead decoding: Jacobi-style parallel n-gram guesses. Prompt-lookup / n-gram: copy from the prompt (great for RAG/summarization).
Math: Compare tree-attention verification (many candidates/pass) vs linear speculation; estimate acceptance gains.
Code: — (n-gram / prompt-lookup speculative draft: propose tokens by matching recent context to the prompt)
Deliverable: prompt_lookup.py + notes

Theory: Force outputs to match a schema/regex/CFG by masking invalid next-token logits at each step (guided/constrained decoding). Outlines/XGrammar/GBNF. Near-zero overhead with compiled FSMs. Critical for tool calling and reliable JSON. Failure modes: tokenization mismatches, over-constraining hurting quality.
Math: Show how a JSON grammar restricts the allowed next-token set at each step; estimate the logit-mask cost.
Code: Implement a simple constrained decoder: mask logits to a token whitelist derived from a regex/FSM state; generate valid JSON.
Deliverable: constrained_decode.py

Theory: Split each layer's weight matrices across GPUs (Megatron-style: column-parallel then row-parallel), all-reduce per layer. Needed when the model doesn't fit on one GPU, and to cut TPOT (weights split → less HBM per GPU to stream). Cost: an all-reduce every layer → needs fast interconnect (NVLink). Best within a node.
Math: 70B fp16 = 140GB → needs TP≥2 on 80GB GPUs. Show TP=4 cuts per-GPU weight read to 35GB → TPOT ≈ 35/2000 = 17.5ms. Count all-reduce bytes per token.
Code: — (TP sharding diagram for one attention + FFN layer; annotate the comm points)
Deliverable: TP diagram + math

Theory: Split layers across GPUs into stages; micro-batches flow through the pipeline. Adds memory headroom but introduces pipeline 'bubbles' that hurt latency — less ideal for low-latency decode than TP. Good across nodes (less comm than TP). Often combined: TP within a node, PP across nodes.
Math: Estimate pipeline bubble fraction = (stages-1)/(micro_batches+stages-1); show why PP suits throughput, TP suits latency.
Code: — (PP vs TP decision notes with the bubble formula)
Deliverable: PP notes

Theory: MoE routes each token to top-k of N experts → only a fraction of params active per token (compute-cheap) but ALL experts must be resident (memory-heavy). Expert parallelism shards experts across GPUs; all-to-all routes tokens to their experts. Load imbalance and all-to-all bandwidth are the serving pain points.
Math: Mixtral 8×7B: 47B total params, ~13B active per token. Show memory needs all 47B resident but compute is ~13B → the serving tradeoff.
Code: — (all-to-all expert routing diagram + active vs total param math)
Deliverable: EP diagram

Theory: Very long context blows up KV cache and attention. Sequence/context parallelism splits the sequence across GPUs; ring attention passes K,V blocks around a ring so each GPU sees all keys without materializing the full matrix. Enables million-token context. Comm-bound.
Math: Show KV cache for 1M-token context is infeasible on one GPU; ring attention distributes it across R GPUs → KV/R each.
Code: — (ring-attention dataflow sketch)
Deliverable: Ring attention notes

Theory: The comms primitives behind all parallelism: all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-to-all. Ring all-reduce bandwidth = α·(N-1)/N. Interconnect tiers: NVLink (intra-node, ~900 GB/s H100) vs PCIe vs InfiniBand (inter-node). Why TP must stay on NVLink and PP can cross nodes.
Math: Ring all-reduce effective BW = α·(N-1)/N × link_BW; latency = O(N) hops. Compute all-reduce time for a TP=8 layer's activations on NVLink.
Code: — (comms primitives + interconnect tier table)
Deliverable: Comms notes

Theory: Tie it all together: OpenAI-compatible API server → tokenizer → scheduler (continuous batching + preemption) → block manager (PagedAttention) → model workers (TP/PP) → sampler → detokenizer/streaming. How a request flows through. PagedAttention + continuous batching are the two ideas that made vLLM.
Math: Trace a request end-to-end and mark where TTFT vs TPOT time is spent and where KV memory is allocated/freed.
Code: Build a mock vLLM: API queue → scheduler (your cont-batch loop) → block allocator → 'model' step → streaming response. Wire your earlier components together.
Deliverable: mini_vllm.py + arch diagram

Theory: SGLang: RadixAttention (automatic prefix KV sharing via a radix tree) + a programming frontend for complex LLM programs (branching, parallelism, constrained decoding). When SGLang's prefix sharing beats vLLM (heavy shared prefixes, agentic/multi-turn). Cache-aware scheduling.
Math: Show the throughput win of RadixAttention on a workload where 90% of requests share a long prefix.
Code: — (compare your prefix_cache.py to RadixAttention; note the radix-tree advantage)
Deliverable: SGLang notes

topic: Engine comparison: vLLM / TensorRT-LLM / TGI / LMDeploy / DeepSpeed
_source:
Theory: vLLM (PagedAttention, easy, broad models), TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, compiled kernels, fastest on NVIDIA, heavier to build), TGI (HuggingFace, production features), LMDeploy (TurboMind), DeepSpeed-MII. How to choose: hardware, model coverage, latency vs ease, quantization support. Owns your 'which engine and why'.
Code: — (decision table: engine × [speed, model support, quant, ease, ecosystem] + a 60s 'which would you pick' answer)
Deliverable: Engine comparison table

Theory: The serving surface: OpenAI-compatible endpoints, SSE token streaming, tokenizer/detokenizer edge cases (partial UTF-8, special tokens), stop sequences, max_tokens, logprobs, request cancellation, timeouts. Tokenization cost and batching of the tokenizer itself.
Code: Wrap your mini engine in a streaming server (yield tokens as generated); handle stop sequences and cancellation.
Deliverable: stream_server.py

topic: torch.compile / CUDA graphs / kernel fusion for inference
_source:
Theory: Reduce Python + kernel-launch overhead (which dominates small-batch decode). CUDA graphs capture and replay the decode step to kill launch overhead. torch.compile fuses ops. Custom fused kernels (fused RMSNorm+matmul, fused sampling). Why these matter most in the memory-bound, launch-overhead-dominated decode regime.
Math: Estimate kernel-launch overhead per decode step (hundreds of small kernels × ~5µs) and the CUDA-graph savings.
Code: — (measure decode step time with/without CUDA graphs conceptually; list fusible ops)
Deliverable: Fusion/graphs notes

topic: Capacity planning — GPUs for a QPS/SLO target
_source:
Theory: The end-to-end sizing question. Given model size, target QPS, input/output length distribution, and TTFT/TPOT SLOs → number and type of GPUs. Combines memory (weights+KV → max concurrency), TPOT (decode BW), and TTFT (prefill compute). The classic senior interview design question.
Math: capacity = f(QPS, tokens/req, TPOT SLO, per-GPU throughput). Work a full example: LLaMA-2 70B, 10 QPS, 500-token outputs, TPOT 30ms → GPU count.
Code: capacity_planner(model_size, slo_ms, qps, in_len, out_len) → GPU count + type; verify the 70B case.
Deliverable: capacity.py + worked example

Theory: Scale replicas on queue depth / GPU-KV utilization (not CPU). Routing: least-loaded, session-affinity (route to the replica holding your prefix cache — cache-aware routing), prefill/decode-aware routing. Cold-start problem (model load = 10s-min → keep warm pools). Handling bursts + overload (shed vs queue).
Math: Show why routing to the replica with your cached prefix beats round-robin (avoids re-prefill); estimate the TTFT difference.
Code: — (autoscaling + routing policy notes; cache-aware routing rationale)
Deliverable: Scaling/routing notes

Theory: $/1M tokens = (GPU $/hr) / (tokens/hr at target SLO). Levers: quantization, batching/goodput, GQA, spec decoding, right-sizing the GPU, spot instances, disaggregation, caching. How to reason about cost vs latency vs quality as a Pareto frontier. Owns your $5K-savings story.
Math: Compute $/1M tokens for 7B on an A100 at measured throughput; show how int8 + better batching moves the number.
Code: cost_per_token(gpu_cost_hr, throughput_tok_s); tabulate the effect of each optimization lever.
Deliverable: cost_model.py

Theory: Serve many fine-tuned LoRA adapters on ONE base model: keep the base resident, swap tiny adapters per request, batch across adapters (S-LoRA: unified paging for adapter weights + heterogeneous batching). Beats loading a full model per tenant. Model swapping / multiplexing for cold models.
Math: Compare memory: N full 7B models (N×14GB) vs 1 base + N LoRA adapters (14GB + N×~40MB). Show the concurrency win.
Code: — (multi-adapter batching sketch: route requests to adapters, batch on the shared base)
Deliverable: S-LoRA notes

Theory: The metrics that matter: TTFT/TPOT/E2E percentiles (p50/p95/p99), queue depth, batch size, KV-cache utilization, preemption rate, GPU MBU/MFU, goodput, tokens/sec, error/timeout rate. Alerting on SLO breach. Load testing. Ties to your production monitoring / 86-metric work.
Code: — (dashboard spec: the 10 inference metrics you'd chart + alert thresholds)
Deliverable: Observability spec

Theory: Deep-dive on separating prefill and decode clusters: independent scaling, per-phase hardware (prefill likes compute, decode likes bandwidth), KV transfer over fast interconnect. Goodput gains and when the KV-transfer cost dominates. State of the art in large deployments.
Math: Model total cost co-located vs disaggregated as prefill/decode ratio varies; find the crossover.
Code: — (deep dive notes on Splitwise/DistServe design choices)
Deliverable: Disagg deep-dive

Theory: When KV won't fit: offload to CPU/NVMe (hierarchical KV, e.g. LMCache) with prefetch, or EVICT tokens. StreamingLLM (attention sinks + recent window) enables infinite streaming. H2O / heavy-hitter eviction keeps only high-attention tokens. Quality vs memory tradeoffs.
Math: Show attention-sink intuition: keeping the first few tokens + a recent window preserves quality at O(window) KV instead of O(n).
Code: Implement a sliding-window + attention-sink KV policy in your decode loop; verify bounded KV memory over a long generation.
Deliverable: streaming_kv.py

Theory: When framework kernels aren't enough: Triton (Python-like, blocks + program_id) for fused softmax, fused RMSNorm, custom paged-attention kernels. CUDA thread hierarchy, shared memory, coalesced access, tiling. The NVIDIA/Meta-infra depth signal.
Code: Triton fused softmax that matches F.softmax to 1e-5 (or numpy pseudocode + tile-size reasoning). Optional: tiled matmul.
Deliverable: fused_softmax.py + tiling note

topic: Design an inference stack (1000 QPS system design)
_source:
Theory: The full mock: design LLM serving for a target QPS/SLO. Cover model+quant choice, GPU sizing (TP/PP), PagedAttention + continuous batching, prefix caching, autoscaling + cache-aware routing, disaggregation if needed, monitoring, cost. Practice the 35-min whiteboard answer end to end.
Math: Full capacity + cost calculation for the chosen scenario, defending every number.
Code: — (whiteboard the full stack from request to token; time it to 35 min)
Deliverable: Inference system-design writeup

Theory: Measure what you've been estimating: send controlled load, record TTFT/TPOT/E2E percentiles, throughput, goodput vs concurrency. Compare batch sizes / quantization / engines. Turns theory into evidence you can cite in interviews.
Math: Validate your TTFT/TPOT/capacity models against measured numbers within 10-20%.
Code: Benchmark script: ramp concurrency against a real engine (or your mini engine), plot throughput vs latency and find the knee.
Deliverable: benchmark.py + latency-throughput curve

topic: Inference formulas & key numbers — from memory
_source:
Theory: Re-write every core inference formula cold: roofline/ridge, arithmetic intensity, KV-cache bytes, TTFT, TPOT, FlashAttention IO, PagedAttention waste, GQA reduction, spec-decoding speedup, cost/token. Plus key hardware numbers (A100/H100 FLOPS + BW). The pre-interview cheat sheet.
Math: Reproduce all formulas + the A100/H100 numbers from memory; redo monthly.
Deliverable: Inference cheat sheet recreated

Theory: The canonical modern recipe: pretrain (next-token) → SFT (instruction following) → preference optimization (RLHF/PPO or DPO) → optional iterative rounds. What each stage buys: SFT teaches format/behavior, preference tuning teaches ranking/values. Base vs instruct vs chat models. Where your voice-bot SFT+DPO pipeline sits.
Code: — (draw the pretrain→SFT→preference→eval pipeline; annotate what data + loss each stage uses)
Deliverable: Pipeline diagram + 60s explainer

topic: When to fine-tune vs RAG vs prompt vs pretrain
_source:
Theory: Decision framework: prompt engineering (fast, no data) → RAG (inject knowledge, reduce hallucination) → fine-tune (change behavior/format/style, distill) → continued pretrain (new domain/language). Cost, latency, data, and maintenance tradeoffs. Fine-tuning teaches BEHAVIOR, not FACTS — the key interview line.
Code: — (build the decision table + a crisp 90s 'when would you fine-tune vs RAG vs prompt' answer)
Deliverable: Decision framework rehearsed

topic: Full fine-tune vs PEFT — the framework
_source:
Theory: Full FT (update all params) vs PEFT (LoRA/adapters, update <1%). Compute, memory, catastrophic forgetting, multi-task/multi-adapter serving, generalization. When full FT is actually worth it (large domain shift, you own the base). Why PEFT dominates in practice.
Math: Contrast trainable params + optimizer memory: full FT 7B = 16P bytes ≈ 112GB; LoRA r=16 ≈ 0.6% trainable, adapter optimizer state tiny.
Code: — (comparison table: full FT vs LoRA vs QLoRA across compute/memory/quality/serving)
Deliverable: Full-FT-vs-PEFT table

Theory: Instruction/response format. Chat templates (system/user/assistant roles, special tokens like <|im_start|>). Why the template MUST match training and inference exactly (mismatch = silent quality loss — your Gemma chat-template fix). Multi-turn formatting. Tool-call formatting.
Code: Implement a chat-template tokenizer: render a multi-turn conversation into token ids with correct role markers; verify round-trip decode.
Deliverable: chat_template.py + round-trip test

Theory: Only ASSISTANT tokens contribute to loss; prompt/user/system tokens get label = -100 (ignored). Why: you don't want the model learning to generate the user's turns. What happens if you don't mask (model degrades, learns to echo prompts). Completion-only vs full-sequence loss.
Math: Show the loss is L = -(1/N_assistant) Σ over assistant tokens only. Demonstrate why including prompt tokens biases the gradient.
Code: Build labels with -100 masking for a multi-turn sample; verify only assistant tokens have non-ignored labels and contribute to CE.
Deliverable: loss_mask.py + verification

Theory: LIMA: 1k high-quality examples beat 50k noisy ones — 'less is more for alignment'. Diversity, deduplication, difficulty balance. Synthetic data (Self-Instruct, Evol-Instruct, distillation from a stronger model). Data contamination / eval leakage. How much data SFT actually needs.
Code: — (write a data-quality checklist + a dedup/near-dup detection sketch)
Deliverable: Data curation notes + checklist

Theory: Format for RLHF/DPO: (prompt, chosen, rejected). How pairs are collected: human ranking, AI feedback (RLAIF), model-vs-model, best-of-n. Inter-annotator agreement. Noise and its effect. On-policy vs off-policy preference data. Why pair quality caps preference-tuning quality.
Code: — (design a preference-collection scheme for your voice bot; note agreement + noise handling)
Deliverable: Preference-data design notes

Theory: Sequence packing (concatenate short samples to fill context, with attention resets so samples don't attend across boundaries) vs padding. Truncation strategy (keep the response). Attention masks. Throughput impact of packing. Position-id resets.
Math: Show packing efficiency gain = 1 - (padded_tokens/total). Compute for a batch with high length variance.
Code: Implement sequence packing with a block-diagonal attention mask + position-id reset; verify samples don't attend across boundaries.
Deliverable: packing.py + mask test

Theory: SFT = causal LM cross-entropy on (masked) assistant tokens. The full loop: forward → CE on assistant tokens → backward → optimizer step. Teacher forcing. Why SFT alone can't exceed the quality of its demonstrations (imitation ceiling) → motivates preference tuning.
Math: Write L_SFT = -Σ_t m_t · log π_θ(y_t | y_<t, x), m_t = assistant mask. Relate to MLE.
Code: Full SFT loop on a tiny model: masked CE, AdamW, cosine LR + warmup, grad clip; log loss. Verify loss decreases and only assistant tokens train.
Deliverable: sft_train.py + loss curve

Theory: Learning rate (SFT typically 1e-5 to 2e-5 full, higher for LoRA), 1-3 epochs (more → overfit/forget), warmup ratio, cosine vs linear decay, batch size + grad accumulation, weight decay, NEFTune noise. How to tell you're overfitting (train loss ↓ but eval/behavior ↓).
Math: Effective batch = micro_batch × grad_accum × n_gpu. Compute the accum steps to hit a target effective batch on limited memory.
Code: Add gradient accumulation to your SFT loop; verify effective batch matches the non-accumulated run's gradients.
Deliverable: grad_accum.py + hp notes

Theory: Fine-tuning erodes pretrained capabilities. Mitigations: lower LR, fewer epochs, LoRA (freezes base), replay/mixing pretrain data, KL/regularization to base, model averaging (model soup / WiSE-FT). How to measure forgetting (eval on general benchmarks before/after).
Math: Show LoRA limits forgetting because base weights are frozen; contrast with full FT weight drift ‖θ_ft - θ_base‖.
Code: — (measure a general-capability proxy before/after a fine-tune; note the drop)
Deliverable: Forgetting notes + measurement

topic: LoRA — math (ΔW=BA, α/r scaling, ΔW=0 init)
_source:
Theory: ΔW = BA, B∈R^{d×r}, A∈R^{r×k}, r ≪ d. Forward: h = W₀x + (α/r)·BAx. Init A~N(0,σ²), B=0 so ΔW=0 at start (training begins from the pretrained model). α/r scaling decouples LR from rank. Low intrinsic-rank hypothesis. Which modules to target (q,k,v,o + MLP).
Math: Show BA=0 at init and becomes nonzero after one gradient step. LoRA params = r·(d_in+d_out). For 7B all-linear r=16 ≈ 0.6% trainable. Show α/r scaling effect on update magnitude.
Code: LoRALinear: freeze base, add A,B with α/r scaling; merge_weights() folds ΔW into W₀. Apply to attention+FFN; verify <2% trainable, only adapters in optimizer.
Deliverable: lora.py + merge fn

topic: QLoRA — NF4 + double quant + paged optimizers
_source:
Theory: Quantize frozen base to 4-bit NF4 (info-optimal for ~N(0,1) weights), keep LoRA adapters in bf16. Double quantization (quantize the quant constants → ~0.4 bits/param saved). Paged optimizers (page 8-bit AdamW state to CPU on spikes). Preserves full-FT quality at a fraction of memory. Your H100 27B story.
Math: Memory: 7B in NF4 ≈ 3.5GB base + r=16 LoRA + paged 8-bit AdamW vs 112GB full bf16 FT. Show adapters <0.5%.
Code: Wrap the base with NF4 fake-quant (dequant on forward), bf16 LoRA on top; verify forward ≈ bf16 within tolerance; only adapters train.
Deliverable: qlora.py + memory table

topic: LoRA variants: DoRA, rsLoRA, VeRA, LoRA+, PiSSA
_source:
Theory: DoRA (decompose into magnitude + direction, closer to full FT). rsLoRA (rank-stabilized scaling α/√r). LoRA+ (different LRs for A and B). VeRA (shared frozen random A,B + tiny trained vectors). PiSSA (init from principal singular components). When each helps and the quality/param tradeoffs.
Math: Compare the scaling factor: LoRA α/r vs rsLoRA α/√r; show why √r stabilizes higher ranks.
Code: — (variants comparison table: idea, extra params, when to use)
Deliverable: LoRA-variants table

topic: Other PEFT: adapters, prefix/prompt tuning, (IA)³, BitFit
_source:
Theory: Bottleneck adapters (Houlsby), prefix tuning (trainable virtual tokens in KV), prompt tuning (soft prompts at input), P-tuning v2, (IA)³ (learned scaling vectors), BitFit (train only biases). How they differ from LoRA (inference overhead, expressiveness). Why LoRA won (mergeable, no inference cost).
Code: — (PEFT taxonomy: where each injects params + inference-time cost)
Deliverable: PEFT taxonomy notes

Theory: One base model + N task adapters swapped per request. S-LoRA: unified paging for adapter weights, heterogeneous batching across adapters. Beats loading N full models. Adapter hot-swap, routing per tenant. Ties inference + fine-tuning together.
Math: Memory: N full 7B (N×14GB) vs 1 base + N adapters (14GB + N×~40MB). Show the multi-tenant win.
Code: — (multi-adapter batching sketch: route requests to adapters, batch on shared base)
Deliverable: Multi-LoRA serving notes

Theory: Train a scalar reward r(x,y) from preference pairs so chosen > rejected. Architecture: base LM + a scalar head on the last token. The RM is the learned proxy for human values that PPO optimizes against. Data format, training, and why the RM is the bottleneck of RLHF.
Math: Derive BT loss = -log σ(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)). Show it decreases as the reward gap grows. Relate to logistic regression on pairs.
Code: rm_loss(r_chosen, r_rejected) + a scalar-head model; verify loss decreases on synthetic pairs where chosen truly better.
Deliverable: rm.py + loss curve

Theory: Optimizing a proxy reward eventually diverges from true quality (Goodhart). Reward over-optimization: KL from ref rises, reward ↑ but human quality ↓ (the classic hump). Length bias, sycophancy, formatting exploits. Why the KL penalty and RM ensembles/uncertainty exist.
Math: Sketch the reward-vs-KL over-optimization curve; explain why gold reward peaks then falls as proxy reward keeps rising.
Code: — (3 concrete reward-hacking examples + mitigations for your voice bot)
Deliverable: Reward-hacking writeup

topic: RM variants: outcome vs process, pairwise vs pointwise
_source:
Theory: Outcome RM (score final answer) vs Process RM / PRM (score each reasoning step — big for math/reasoning, o1-style). Pairwise (BT) vs pointwise (regression) vs listwise. Absolute-score RMs. LLM-as-judge as an implicit RM. Where process rewards changed reasoning training.
Code: — (table: RM types, label needs, where each wins; note PRM for reasoning)
Deliverable: RM variants notes

topic: RLHF objective + KL penalty (the core equation)
_source:
Theory: max_π E_{x,y~π}[r(x,y)] - β·KL(π_θ || π_ref). Reward from the RM minus a per-token KL penalty keeping the policy near the SFT reference (prevents reward hacking + preserves fluency). β controls the tradeoff (β→0 free rein, β→∞ frozen). The equation every alignment interview wants.
Math: Derive the optimal policy π*(y|x) ∝ π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x,y)/β) from the KL-regularized objective (this is also the seed of the DPO derivation).
Code: — (paper derivation of π* + explain the role of β with two limits)
Deliverable: RLHF objective derivation

topic: PPO — actors, critics, and the four models
_source:
Theory: The RLHF PPO setup runs FOUR models: policy (actor, trained), value model (critic, trained), reward model (frozen), reference (frozen, for KL). Rollout → score → advantage → update. Why this is memory-heavy and finicky. The full data flow.
Math: Reward signal per token: R_t = r_RM at final token - β·KL(π_θ||π_ref) per token. Show where the value head's baseline reduces variance.
Code: — (draw the PPO-RLHF loop: rollout, reward+KL, GAE, clipped update; label all 4 models)
Deliverable: PPO-RLHF flow diagram

Theory: Clipped surrogate stops destructive large policy updates. GAE trades bias/variance in advantage estimation. Ratio r_t = π_θ/π_old. Epochs over each rollout batch. Value-function clipping, entropy bonus. Why clipping (vs a trust region / KL constraint).
Math: L^CLIP = E[min(r_t·A_t, clip(r_t,1-ε,1+ε)·A_t)]. GAE: A_t = Σ_l (γλ)^l δ_{t+l}, δ_t = R_t + γV(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t). Show clipping bounds the update.
Code: ppo_clip_loss(logp_new, logp_old, adv, eps) + gae(rewards, values, gamma, lam); verify clipping activates when ratio leaves [1-ε,1+ε].
Deliverable: ppo.py + GAE test

Theory: Instability sources: RM drift, KL collapse/explosion, reward hacking, value-model init, mode collapse (low diversity), length bias. Tricks: adaptive KL controller, reward whitening/normalization, advantage normalization, careful LR, warmup, clip range. Why RLHF is hard to reproduce.
Math: Adaptive KL controller: β_{t+1} = β_t·(1 + K_β·(KL_actual/KL_target - 1)); show it targets a KL budget.
Code: — (implement reward whitening + advantage normalization; note the stability effect)
Deliverable: RLHF stability notes

topic: Critic-free RL basics: REINFORCE, RLOO, ReMax
_source:
Theory: Simpler-than-PPO methods that drop the value model. REINFORCE + baseline (high variance). RLOO (leave-one-out baseline from k samples — no critic). ReMax (greedy-baseline). These set up the GRPO family (next section), which generalizes the 'baseline from a group of samples' idea. Why removing the critic saves memory + tuning.
Math: RLOO baseline = mean of the other k−1 rewards: A_{k}=r_k − (1/(k−1))Σ_{i≠k} r_i. Show it is an unbiased, critic-free advantage.
Code: Implement GRPO group-relative advantages for k completions of one prompt; verify zero-mean per group.
Deliverable: grpo.py + advantage test

Theory: DeepSeek's GRPO (DeepSeekMath → DeepSeek-R1) — the method that powered the reasoning-RL wave. Drops PPO's value model entirely: for each prompt sample a GROUP of K completions (8-64), use the group's mean reward as the baseline → advantage = z-scored reward within the group, shared across all tokens of a response. Halves memory, removes the noisy critic. Per-token importance ratio + PPO-style clip + KL to ref. Pairs naturally with verifiable rewards (RLVR).
Math: Â_k = (r_k − mean(r_group))/std(r_group), same for every token of response k. J = E[(1/K)Σ_k (1/|o_k|)Σ_t min(ρ_{k,t}Â_k, clip(ρ_{k,t},1±ε)Â_k) − β·KL(π_θ‖π_ref)], ρ_{k,t}=π_θ/π_old. Show no V(s) is needed and advantages are zero-mean per group.
Code: Implement GRPO: sample K completions, compute group-normalized advantages, per-token clipped surrogate + KL. Verify advantages zero-mean per group; confirm no critic model exists.
Deliverable: grpo.py + advantage test

Theory: 'GRPO Done Right' (Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training). GRPO's normalizers inject biases: (1) dividing by response length |o_k| makes the model prefer LONGER wrong answers and SHORTER right ones → the reward-independent response-length inflation seen in R1-Zero; (2) dividing by group std over-weights easy vs hard questions (difficulty bias); (3) 1/K vs 1/(K−1) baseline scaling. Dr. GRPO drops the length + std normalization → unbiased optimization, kills the length-inflation artifact.
Math: GRPO divides by |o_k| and std[r]. Dr. GRPO: A_k = r_k − mean(r_group) (NO /std, NO /|o_k|). Show why /|o_k| incentivizes length and /std distorts per-question gradients; the 1/(K−1) fix is absorbed into the LR.
Code: Modify your GRPO → Dr. GRPO (remove length + std normalization). Show the response-length-inflation artifact disappears on a toy run.
Deliverable: dr_grpo.py + bias note

Theory: ByteDance/Tsinghua 2025, fully open — 'GRPO with the lessons from running it at scale'; trained Qwen2.5-32B to AIME-50 with ~50% fewer steps than R1-Zero. Four tricks: (1) CLIP-HIGHER — decouple and raise the UPPER clip bound so low-prob tokens still update → prevents entropy collapse, preserves exploration; (2) DYNAMIC SAMPLING — drop prompts whose K rollouts are all-correct or all-wrong (zero advantage = zero gradient) and resample → informative batches only; (3) TOKEN-LEVEL policy-gradient loss (sum over all tokens, not mean-per-sequence) so long CoT avoids vanishing gradients; (4) OVERLONG REWARD SHAPING — soft length penalty to denoise truncated responses.
Math: Asymmetric clip: min(ρÂ, clip(ρ, 1−ε_low, 1+ε_high)Â) with ε_high>ε_low. Token-level loss = (1/Σ_k|o_k|)Σ_k Σ_t (...) vs GRPO's (1/K)Σ_k(1/|o_k|)Σ_t. Explain each trick's failure mode fixed.
Code: Extend GRPO with clip-higher (asymmetric ε) + dynamic-sampling filter (drop all-same-reward groups) + token-level normalization. Verify all-correct/all-wrong groups are filtered out.
Deliverable: dapo.py + 4-tricks note

Theory: Qwen Team/Alibaba (Qwen3). GRPO's per-TOKEN importance ratio is high-variance and mismatched — the advantage is sequence-level but the ratio is token-level — causing instability, worst for MoE and long sequences. GSPO uses a SEQUENCE-level importance ratio (length-normalized geometric mean of token likelihoods) and clips/weights the whole response → much more stable RL, better MoE training, cleaner scaling. The macro trend: token-level (GRPO) → sequence-level (GSPO).
Math: Sequence ratio s_k = (π_θ(o_k|q)/π_old(o_k|q))^{1/|o_k|} (length-normalized geometric mean). Objective clips at sequence level: min(s_k Â_k, clip(s_k,1±ε)Â_k). Contrast variance with GRPO's per-token ρ_{k,t}.
Code: Implement GSPO's sequence-level ratio + clipped objective; compare gradient variance to token-level GRPO on identical rollouts.
Deliverable: gspo.py + variance comparison

Theory: The 'how exactly do we clip/weight' refinements around GRPO. CISPO (MiniMax M1): clip the IMPORTANCE-SAMPLING weight instead of masking token updates → keeps every token's gradient, faster convergence than GRPO. REINFORCE++ (global-batch baseline + PPO-style stabilizers, no groups). KL-Cov / Clip-Cov: covariance-based clipping to control entropy/exploration. Know these as the variant space, not necessarily to implement each.
Math: CISPO: apply clip to the IS weight ρ but RETAIN its gradient (no min-of-two masking that zeroes tokens). REINFORCE++ baseline = global batch-mean reward.
Code: — (comparison table: what each clips/weights vs GRPO; token vs weight vs sequence)
Deliverable: Clipping-variants table

topic: PRIME — process rewards via implicit RM
_source:
Theory: PRIME-RL: online RL with PROCESS (per-step) rewards WITHOUT training a separately step-labeled PRM. Derive an implicit token-level process reward from an OUTCOME-trained reward model (implicit PRM) and update it online → dense credit assignment for reasoning while avoiding the cost + label-noise of an explicit PRM. Plugs into GRPO-style policy optimization. Part of the 'dense reward for reasoning' push.
Math: Implicit process reward at token t ∝ β·log(π_RM/π_ref) — a dense per-token signal vs sparse outcome-only reward. Show denser credit assignment reduces variance on long CoT.
Code: — (design an implicit-PRM reward: token-level from an outcome RM; feed as dense reward into GRPO)
Deliverable: PRIME design notes

topic: VAPO, GFPO & how to decode any new *PO
_source:
Theory: VAPO — value-AUGMENTED PO: brings a well-tuned value model back for reliable long-CoT RL, competitive with critic-free methods (the pendulum swinging partway back). GFPO — Group-Filtered PO (filter which group samples contribute). New '*PO' variants land constantly. Frameworks (verl, TRL) support PPO/GRPO/GSPO/DAPO/Dr.GRPO/ReMax/REINFORCE++/RLOO/PRIME out of the box — so the skill is DECODING a new method fast, not memorizing all.
Code: — (decode-any-new-method checklist: baseline/advantage? clip token vs seq vs weight? critic or not? outcome vs process reward? on/off-policy?)
Deliverable: Method-decoder checklist

Theory: The key result: the KL-constrained RLHF optimum can be solved WITHOUT RL. Start from π* ∝ π_ref·exp(r/β), invert to express r in terms of π*, substitute into the Bradley-Terry loss → a simple classification loss on preference pairs. No RM, no rollouts, no value model. Why it's stable and cheap. When it underperforms PPO (off-policy, distribution shift).
Math: Do the FULL derivation cold, twice: (1) RLHF max → π*(y|x)=π_ref·exp(r/β)/Z, (2) solve r(x,y)=β·log(π*/π_ref)+β·log Z, (3) sub into BT loss → Z cancels → DPO loss.
Code: — (write the complete derivation on paper; the Z-cancellation is the crux)
Deliverable: Full DPO derivation (cold ×2)

Theory: Implicit reward r(x,y) = β·log(π_θ(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)). Loss pushes chosen's implicit reward above rejected's. Reference model (frozen) computes ref logps. Typical β=0.1-0.5. The gradient up-weights rejected-when-wrong. What each term does. Your voice-bot DPO pipeline.
Math: L_DPO = -E[log σ(β(log π_θ(y_w|x)/π_ref(y_w|x) - log π_θ(y_l|x)/π_ref(y_l|x)))]. Show ∂L/∂θ scales by the reward-estimate error. Show loss decreases as chosen-rejected gap grows.
Code: dpo_loss(policy_chosen_logps, policy_rejected_logps, ref_chosen_logps, ref_rejected_logps, beta); verify decreases as gap grows; verify =−log σ(0) at init when policy=ref.
Deliverable: dpo_loss.py + verify

Theory: Likelihood of BOTH chosen and rejected can drop (DPO reduces rejected faster than it raises chosen). Sensitivity to β and to reference model. Off-policy data mismatch. Overfitting on easy pairs. Length exploitation. Needs SFT first (DPO on a base model is unstable). Loss-masking + logp computation bugs (your real debugging story).
Math: Show why margin can grow while both logps fall (only the DIFFERENCE is constrained). Contrast with methods that anchor absolute logp.
Code: — (add a diagnostic logging chosen/rejected logps + margin over training; spot the both-fall pattern)
Deliverable: DPO diagnostics + gotchas

topic: DPO variants: IPO, cDPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO, R-DPO
_source:
Theory: IPO (fixes DPO overfitting, drops the BT assumption). cDPO (label smoothing for noisy prefs). KTO (uses unpaired good/bad labels — no pairs needed, prospect-theory loss). ORPO (SFT + odds-ratio preference in ONE stage, no ref model). SimPO (reference-free, length-normalized reward). R-DPO (length regularized). When each wins.
Math: SimPO reward = (β/|y|)·log π_θ(y|x) (length-normalized, no ref) + a target margin γ. ORPO adds λ·log-odds-ratio penalty to the SFT loss. Contrast ref-free vs ref-based.
Code: Implement SimPO loss (length-normalized, reference-free, margin γ); compare its gradient to DPO on the same pair.
Deliverable: simpo.py + variants table

topic: Self-play & game-theoretic preference (SPIN, SPPO, Nash, BOND)
_source:
Theory: Beyond pairwise DPO. SPIN (self-play FT: the model's own generations are negatives vs human positives, iterate — no preference labels needed). SPPO (self-play preference optimization toward a Nash equilibrium). Nash-MD / NLHF (frame RLHF as a two-player game → Nash policy; handles intransitive/non-BT preferences). BOND (Best-of-N Distillation: get best-of-N quality without N× inference by distilling the BoN policy). When these beat vanilla DPO.
Math: SPPO pushes toward the Nash equilibrium of the preference game (drops BT's transitivity assumption). BOND matches the best-of-N distribution via distribution matching (e.g. Jeffreys divergence).
Code: — (SPIN iteration sketch: current model's samples = negatives, human answers = positives, SFT-style loop)
Deliverable: Self-play methods notes

Theory: Train a small student to match a large teacher. Logit distillation: KL(student || teacher) on soft targets with temperature T. Sequence-level KD (train on teacher generations). Combine with CE on ground truth. Why soft targets carry 'dark knowledge'. Distilling a fine-tuned/aligned teacher into a deployable student.
Math: L = α·T²·KL(σ(z_s/T) || σ(z_t/T)) + (1-α)·CE(y, σ(z_s)). Explain the T² gradient-scaling term and temperature's effect on soft targets.
Code: distill_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, labels, T, alpha); verify the soft-target term dominates at high T.
Deliverable: distill.py + T ablation

Theory: Where memory goes: weights 2P + grads 2P + Adam states 12P = 16P bytes + activations. bf16 (no loss scaler) vs fp16 (needs GradScaler). Master weights. How LoRA/QLoRA collapse the 16P term. The calc behind 'will it fit'.

Math: Checkpointing memory ≈ O(√N) activations vs O(N); show the ~33% compute overhead tradeoff.
Code: Add torch.utils.checkpoint to your training block; measure peak-memory drop vs the added step time.
Deliverable: checkpointing.py + benchmark

topic: Evaluating a fine-tuned model (no ground truth)
_source:
Theory: The hard part: how do you know it improved? Held-out benchmarks, LLM-as-judge (pairwise win-rate vs baseline), human eval, task-specific metrics, capability regression checks (MMLU etc.), reward/KL curves. Avoiding eval gaming + contamination. Your DeepEval 3-model pipeline + 86-metric taxonomy.
Math: Pairwise win-rate + confidence interval; note position/verbosity bias in LLM-as-judge and how to debias (swap order, length-control).
Code: — (design an eval harness: baseline vs fine-tuned, LLM-judge win-rate with position-swap, regression suite)
Deliverable: Eval harness design
